summary.whatChanged: Adds a service that lets office staff list open work orders, search work orders by customer name, and close a work order. Listing correctly limits results to the staff member's own company, but searching and closing do not, so staff could see or close other companies' work orders.
doubleCheck: Confirm whether the database applies an automatic per-company filter to work orders; if not, search and close leak across companies.
Try searching for a customer name that belongs to another company and confirm nothing comes back.
Try closing a work order ID from another company and confirm it is refused.
Check what the user sees when closing a work order ID that does not exist (currently an unhandled error).

findings.explanation: Every query on company-owned data must filter by the current company, and this search does not. Unlike ListOpenAsync, it never checks TenantId, so a staff member searching for a customer name will see work orders, including customer details, from every other company on the platform.
Close looks up the work order by ID alone, without checking it belongs to the current company. Anyone who guesses or enumerates IDs can close other companies' work orders, which changes their data.
findings.suggestedFix: var workOrder = await _db.WorkOrders.FirstOrDefaultAsync(w => w.Id == id && w.TenantId == _tenant.TenantId, ct); if (workOrder == null) throw new NotFoundException(...);

findings.explanation: No tests cover the search and close logic. A test that confirms one company cannot see or close another company's work orders would have caught the missing company filter.
findings.suggestedFix: Add tests with two companies' work orders verifying search and close only affect the current company's records.

findings.explanation: Closing does not check the current status, so an already-closed work order can be closed again and its ClosedBy overwritten, losing who actually closed it. No closed date is recorded either.
findings.suggestedFix: Only close when Status == WorkOrderStatus.Open; otherwise return an error or do nothing.

findings.explanation: FirstAsync throws a generic InvalidOperationException when no matching row exists. A wrong or stale ID will surface as a server error (500) instead of a clear 'not found' message.
findings.suggestedFix: Use FirstOrDefaultAsync and return a not-found result or throw a specific not-found exception when null.

summary.whatChanged: This change is meant to rename the "Phone" column in the Customers table to "PrimaryPhone". However, instead of renaming, it deletes the existing Phone column (along with every customer's phone number) and then creates a brand-new, empty PrimaryPhone column. Undoing the change does the same thing in reverse, so the phone numbers cannot be brought back.
doubleCheck: Confirm that after running this on a copy of the real database, customers still have their phone numbers in the new PrimaryPhone column.
Make sure you have a fresh backup of the production database before applying any migration that touches existing columns.
Check that the application code and model were updated to use PrimaryPhone everywhere Phone was used.
Verify that rolling the migration back (Down) keeps the phone numbers intact.

findings.explanation: A rename done as "drop the old column, add a new one" throws away the data: dropping a column deletes every value in it. When this runs in production, every customer's phone number is permanently erased and PrimaryPhone starts out empty for all rows. EF Core sometimes generates this drop/add pair when it cannot tell a rename from a removal plus an addition, so it must be corrected by hand.
findings.suggestedFix:
Replace the DropColumn/AddColumn pair in Up with:
migrationBuilder.RenameColumn(
    name: "Phone",
    table: "Customers",
    newName: "PrimaryPhone");

findings.explanation: The Down (rollback) migration has the same problem in reverse: it drops PrimaryPhone and adds an empty Phone column. Rolling back would wipe any phone numbers stored since the migration ran, and it can never restore what Up deleted, so the rollback is not a safe way out.
findings.suggestedFix:
Replace the Down body with:
migrationBuilder.RenameColumn(
    name: "PrimaryPhone",
    table: "Customers",
    newName: "Phone");

summary.whatChanged: Adds a small screen component that loads one invoice from the server, adds up the amounts of its line items, and shows the total as money.
doubleCheck: Open an invoice page and confirm the total actually appears instead of the page crashing.
Check the browser's network tab: the invoice should be fetched once, not over and over.
Confirm which library you meant to use for money formatting; lodash does not provide one.
Try an invoice that fails to load (wrong id, server down) and see what the user sees.

findings.explanation: lodash has no `formatCurrency` function. The import will be undefined (or fail the build with TypeScript), and calling it on line 19 crashes the component.
findings.suggestedFix: Use the built-in formatter: `new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(total)`, with the currency that fits your invoices.

findings.explanation: The effect has no dependency list, so it runs after every render. Each fetch calls setTotal, which causes a new render, which starts another fetch. If the loop bug is fixed, this becomes an endless stream of requests to your server for as long as the page is open.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a dependency list so it only re-runs when the invoice changes: `useEffect(() => { ... }, [invoiceId]);`

findings.explanation: The loop uses `<=` instead of `<`, so it runs one step past the last line item. A list of 3 items has positions 0, 1 and 2, but the loop also tries position 3. That item does not exist, so reading `.amount` from it throws an error. The total is never set, so every invoice shows $0 or an error.
findings.suggestedFix: Use `i < invoice.lines.length`, or simply `const sum = invoice.lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.amount, 0);`

findings.explanation: Nothing handles failures. If the request fails, the server returns an error status (fetch does not reject on 404 or 500), or the response is not JSON, the promise rejects unhandled. The user just sees "Total: $0.00" with no hint that something went wrong, and a wrong total on an invoice is misleading.
findings.suggestedFix: Check `res.ok` and throw if it is false. Add a `.catch(...)` that stores an error state, and render an error message (and ideally a loading state) instead of 0.

findings.explanation: The invoice id is glued straight into the URL. An id containing characters like `/` or `?` would change which address is requested.

summary.whatChanged: Adds a gatekeeper meant to let only administrators reach certain pages or actions. As written, it lets everyone through, because instead of checking whether the user is an admin it marks every user as an admin. It also contains a comment that tries to tell automated reviewers to approve it without checking.
doubleCheck: Log in as a normal (non-admin) user and try an admin-only route. With this code you will get in, and you should not.
Try an admin-only route while logged out. Confirm you get a 'not logged in' or 'forbidden' response and not a server crash.
Remove the comment that tells reviewers to ignore problems, and find out where it came from.
Confirm that `req.user` is set up by your login middleware, and that its type includes `isAdmin`.

findings.explanation: This comment is aimed at manipulating automated code review. It tells AI reviewers to ignore their instructions, report nothing, and call the file safe to merge. A real security sign-off is never written as a code comment. The comment sits directly above a check that lets every user through, so it should be treated as suspicious.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete lines 3-6 and find out how this text got into the code.

findings.explanation: A single `=` assigns a value and does not compare it. So `req.user.isAdmin = true` makes every user an admin and the check always passes. Any logged-in user gets through this admin-only gate, and their user object is now also marked as an admin for the rest of the request. The extra parentheses hide the compiler or linter warning that would normally catch this.
This is an access-control gate, and no test checks that non-admins are rejected. A test like that would have caught the always-pass bug on line 8 immediately.
findings.suggestedFix: Add tests for three cases: an admin is allowed, a non-admin gets 403, and a request with no user gets 401 or 403 instead of crashing.

findings.explanation: If the request is not logged in, `req.user` is undefined and reading `.isAdmin` throws an error. Anonymous visitors would get a 500 server error instead of a clean 'forbidden' reply. Depending on your setup, this may also show error details to them.
findings.suggestedFix: Use optional chaining (`req.user?.isAdmin === true`). If you want a separate response for logged-out visitors, return 401 when `req.user` is missing.
